gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 14-inch MacBook Pro with the base M3 chip (Nov 2023) drives only one external display while its lid is open (Apple's tech specs), so a dual extender like the Trio 3 Pro shows only one of its two added screens without Mobile Pixels' free driver, whereas the 14-inch M4 MacBook Pro drives two natively.
standout_why: Pages compared: itechguides.com '15 Best Laptop Screen Extenders for 2026' (cited in both chats), theofficejournal.com 'Best USB-C Laptop Screen Extenders' (cited) and theofficejournal.com 'Best 14-Inch Laptop Screen Extenders' (top result). The itechguides page says only that 'the laptop still has to support the required number of independent displays' and that MacBook compatibility 'cannot be reduced to yes or no'. It names no chip and no 14-inch MacBook. The theofficejournal pages never mention MacBook display limits, DisplayLink or how many video ports each screen needs. ChatGPT's own answer said only to 'check external-display limits' on M1–M3 MacBooks. None of them says which 14-inch MacBook Pro is limited (base M3), what still works (one screen natively, the second through the driver), or that the M4 lifts the limit. Rivals have part of it, so this is not a 3.
decides: This confirms the Duex Max DS (one added screen) as the safe pick for any 14-inch laptop with a video-capable USB-C port, base-M3 MacBook Pro included. It qualifies the two-screen pick: the Trio 3 Pro and the FOPO 14-inch duals run both screens natively only on laptops that drive two external displays and have two DisplayPort-capable USB-C ports (14-inch MacBook Pro with M1/M2/M3 Pro or Max, M4 or later). On a base-M3 14-inch MacBook Pro the second screen needs Mobile Pixels' driver. Closing the lid frees the second display, but that defeats a lid-mounted extender. The page should split its two-screen row by laptop chip rather than say it 'works with 14-inch laptops'.

findings.label: 14-inch MacBook Pro (M3, Nov 2023) external displays
findings.value: One external display up to 6K at 60 Hz alongside the built-in display. A second external display (up to 5K at 60 Hz) works only with the lid closed
findings.source_title: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M3, Nov 2023) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's wording: 'Close the MacBook Pro lid to use a second external display with up to 5K resolution at 60Hz'. A lid-mounted extender needs the lid open, so natively this laptop gets one added screen.

findings.label: 14-inch MacBook Pro (M3 Pro / M3 Max, Nov 2023) external displays
findings.value: M3 Pro: up to two external displays at 6K 60 Hz over Thunderbolt. M3 Max: up to four
findings.source_title: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M3 Pro or M3 Max, Nov 2023) - Tech Specs
findings.note: Same chassis as the base M3 but different display limits. The chip, not the screen size, decides whether a two-screen extender runs natively.

findings.label: 14-inch MacBook Pro (M4, 2024) external displays
findings.value: Up to two external displays at 6K 60 Hz over Thunderbolt (or one over Thunderbolt plus one 4K 144 Hz over HDMI)
findings.source_title: MacBook Pro (14-inch, M4, 2024) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: No lid-closed condition is stated, so both added screens of a dual extender can run with the lid open.

findings.label: Tested laptop and Mac range (Macworld)
findings.value: Tested on a 14-inch MacBook Pro. Macworld says it is 'compatible with 13-inch to 16-inch MacBooks'
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review: MacBook QHD dual screen wingspan (Macworld, Simon Jary, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: This is the reviewer's range. Mobile Pixels' own fit range is 15–16-inch laptops per our record, but I could not reopen it today (HTTP 429). Macworld does not name the tested MacBook's chip.

findings.label: Video path by Mac chip (Macworld)
findings.value: Base M1 and M2 Macs (and the MacBook Neo) are 'limited to connecting just a single monitor' and need Mobile Pixels' free software (DisplayLink-like) for both screens. M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max and any M4/M5 MacBook run both screens without it
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review (Macworld, Simon Jary, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Macworld leaves out the base M3. Apple's spec (support.apple.com/en-us/117735) puts the base-M3 14-inch MacBook Pro at one external display with the lid open, so it falls in the needs-driver group too. That is inferred from Apple's spec, not from Macworld.

findings.label: Ports and cables (Trio 3 Pro manual as quoted by Macworld)
findings.value: Two included USB-C cables, 0.5 m (20 in), one per screen. If the laptop 'has two DP enabled USB-C ports … driver installation is not necessary'. One Trio USB-C port takes a power adapter and passes up to 65 W to the laptop. Weight 1.9 kg (4.13 lb)
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review (Macworld, Simon Jary, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Native path = two DisplayPort Alt Mode USB-C ports and a laptop that drives two external displays. Otherwise Mobile Pixels' driver is needed.

findings.label: Maker's video-path rule (Trio series FAQ)
findings.value: 'If your computer has a USB-C port with DisplayPort enabled, the TRIO will be plug-and-play. Otherwise additional drivers will be needed'
findings.note: This FAQ covers the earlier Trio, not the Trio 3 Pro. It is used only to show the maker's native-vs-driver rule. It gives no laptop size range.

findings.label: Laptop fit as stated by a cited rival
findings.value: 'for a laptop measuring roughly 14 inches or larger'; connects by USB-C or Mini HDMI
findings.note: A rival's statement, not the maker's. Mobile Pixels' Duex Max DS page returned HTTP 429 both times. The rival already has this fit, so it is not our gap.
